Section 1.1: Thinking Like a Physicist

Learning target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

WTC

What’s to Come

WTC · DOK 3 · data · U1-MG01

A class observes a toy cart on a track. They record the table below.

Time (s)Position (m)
00.00
10.42
20.83
31.25

Connected task: (a) List two observations from the table. (b) Give one inference that is reasonable but not directly observed. (c) Write one testable claim about the cart’s motion. (d) State what additional evidence would help test the claim.

Answer / solution

Observations come directly from the table, such as the recorded positions. A reasonable inference is that the cart moved at an approximately steady rate. A testable claim could be that the cart travels about 0.42 m each second over this interval. Additional repeated position-time measurements would test it.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Exact I-can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Evidence/job: 1.1-WTC

Mastery Goal: U1-MG01 — Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.1 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Notes Example

Example 1

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG01

A cart’s position is recorded as 0.50 m at 2 s. A student says the cart must be speeding up. Identify one observation/measurement and one inference.

Answer / solution

The recorded position is an observation/measurement; “must be speeding up” is an inference not established by one measurement.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Exact I-can: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.

Evidence/job: 1.1-observation/inference

Mastery Goal: U1-MG01 — Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.1 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 4

Notes Example · DOK 2 · mixed · U1-MG01

Measurement
Cart A travels 0.8 m in 1 s
Cart A travels 1.6 m in 2 s
Cart A travels 2.4 m in 3 s
Answer / solution

The measurements support a constant average rate over these intervals; they do not by themselves prove why the rate is constant.

Section 1.2: Forces and Newton’s First Law

Learning target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

WTC

What’s to Come

WTC · DOK 3 · diagram · U1-MG02

Connected task: A book remains at rest on a table. (a) Identify the two shown interactions. (b) Predict what would happen if the support force disappeared while weight remained. (c) Explain why “forces are acting” and “net force is zero” can both be true before the table is removed.

Answer / solution

The shown forces are weight downward and table support upward. Initially they balance, so net force is zero and the book can remain at rest. If support disappears while weight remains, the net force is downward and the book’s velocity changes downward.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Exact I-can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Evidence/job: 1.2-WTC

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.2 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Notes Example

Example 1

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

A puck glides in a straight line at constant speed while horizontal forces balance. Predict what happens next using Newton’s First Law.

Answer / solution

Its velocity remains constant; zero net force means no change in velocity.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Exact I-can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Evidence/job: 1.2-newton1-prediction

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.2 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 2

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

“A heavy box has more inertia force than a light box.” Critique the statement and replace it with correct physics.

Answer / solution

Greater mass means greater inertia, but inertia itself is a property of matter, not a force.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Exact I-can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Evidence/job: 1.2-inertia-misconception

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.2 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 3

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

Two students pull equally hard in opposite directions on a ring. Does this illustrate “no forces acting” or “no net force acting”? Explain.

Answer / solution

Two forces act; the net force is zero, so “no net force” does not mean “no forces.”

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Exact I-can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Evidence/job: 1.2-no-force-vs-zero-net

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.2 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 4

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

A 600 N object rests on a level horizontal surface. Ignoring other vertical interactions, what upward support force acts on it?

Answer / solution

600 N upward, because vertical equilibrium requires the support force to balance the 600 N weight.

Section 1.3: Net Force and Vectors

Learning target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

WTC

What’s to Come

WTC · DOK 3 · diagram · U1-MG03

Connected task: (a) Use arrow direction and magnitude to find the resultant. (b) Sketch or describe a single vector that could replace the two shown horizontal forces. (c) Predict the direction in which the object’s velocity would begin to change if these were the only horizontal forces.

Answer / solution

The resultant is 25 N right. A single 25 N rightward arrow is equivalent for net-force purposes. The velocity would change in the rightward direction.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

Exact I-can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Evidence/job: 1.3-WTC

Mastery Goal: U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.3 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Question 1

Practice Set 1 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG03

Two horizontal forces act to the right: 18 N and 7 N. Find the resultant force.

Answer / solution

25 N to the right.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

Exact I-can: I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.

Evidence/job: 1.3-same-direction-sum

Mastery Goal: U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.3 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Practice Set 1 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG03

Question 3

Practice Set 1 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG03

A scaled force diagram shows one arrow 2 cm left and another 6 cm right. Without converting the scale, state the resultant direction and explain how arrow length matters.

Answer / solution

The resultant points right; the longer arrow has the larger magnitude.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

Exact I-can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Evidence/job: 1.3-arrow-length

Mastery Goal: U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.3 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Exact target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

Evidence/job: U1-1.3-ETA-E4

Mastery Goal: U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Section 1.4: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion

Learning target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

WTC

What’s to Come

WTC · DOK 3 · diagram · U1-MG02

Connected task: Both signs are motionless. (a) State the net force on each sign. (b) Explain how the angled supports in Situation B can still produce equilibrium. (c) Describe one change that would make either sign leave equilibrium.

Answer / solution

Each sign has net force 0 N. In Situation B, horizontal tension components cancel while vertical components combine to balance weight. Any unbalanced change in support or weight would produce a nonzero net force and change the motion.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

Exact I-can: I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

Evidence/job: 1.4-WTC

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.4 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Question 7

Practice Set 3 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

A crate is in horizontal equilibrium. One force is 62 N right and another is 22 N left. What additional leftward force is required?

40 N left.

Section 1.5: Modeling Forces in the Real World

Learning target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

WTC

What’s to Come

WTC · DOK 3 · diagram · U1-MG04

Connected task: The scenario says the crate moves right at constant speed. (a) Determine the net force shown by the arrows. (b) Decide whether the model is consistent with the motion. (c) Revise the model so the representations agree. (d) Explain what evidence from the motion guided your revision.

Answer / solution

The shown net force is 40 N right, which is inconsistent with constant straight-line velocity. Revise the horizontal forces so they balance, such as 80 N right and 80 N left. The key evidence is the constant velocity, which requires zero net force.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Evidence/job: 1.5-WTC

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Notes Example

Example 1

Notes Example · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG04

A laptop rests on a desk. Choose the object as the system and list the external forces that belong on its force diagram.

Answer / solution

Forces on the laptop: weight downward and support force from the desk upward.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.

Evidence/job: 1.5-force-model-construct

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 2

Notes Example · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

The cart rolls at constant speed after a push. Critique the shown force model and describe a revision consistent with the motion.

Answer / solution

A constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. A lone forward force would predict acceleration. Remove the forward force if the push has ended, or include a balancing backward force if a forward interaction continues; also include vertical weight/support as appropriate.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Evidence/job: 1.5-model-critique

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Example 3

Notes Example · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

Do the scenario, motion description, and force model agree? Identify the mismatch and revise one representation.

Answer / solution

They do not agree. The diagram has a 40 N net force right, which would change the velocity. For constant straight-line speed, revise the forces so the horizontal net is 0 N, such as 80 N right and 80 N left.

Alignment / evidence

Question 2

Practice Set 1 · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

The cart rolls at constant speed after a push. Critique the shown force model and describe a revision consistent with the motion.

Answer / solution

A constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. A lone forward force would predict acceleration. Remove the forward force if the push has ended, or include a balancing backward force if a forward interaction continues; also include vertical weight/support as appropriate.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

The force model should have a net force to the right.

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

Question 5

Practice Set 2 · DOK 3 · text · U1-MG04

A student draws “motion force” forward on a coasting cart. Identify the modeling error and revise the force diagram description.

Answer / solution

Motion is not a force. Include only actual interactions; a coasting cart can move with zero net force.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Question 6

Practice Set 2 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG04

A ball moves at constant speed but curves left. Use the motion evidence to decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

Answer / solution

The direction of velocity changes, so the net force is nonzero and points toward the change in direction.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

Question 7

Practice Set 2 · DOK 3 · text · U1-MG04

A hanging plant basket is motionless while two chains pull upward at angles. Describe a defensible force model and connect it to the motion evidence.

Answer / solution

A defensible model includes the basket’s weight downward and two tension forces along the chains; their horizontal components cancel and vertical components balance the weight.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Question 10

Practice Set 2 · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

The cart rolls at constant speed after a push. Critique the shown force model and describe a revision consistent with the motion.

Answer / solution

A constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. A lone forward force would predict acceleration. Remove the forward force if the push has ended, or include a balancing backward force if a forward interaction continues; also include vertical weight/support as appropriate.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Forces on the sled include weight down, support up, pull right, and friction left.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.

Evidence/job: 1.5-force-model-construct

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Question 18

Practice Set 3 · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

The cart rolls at constant speed after a push. Critique the shown force model and describe a revision consistent with the motion.

Answer / solution

A constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. A lone forward force would predict acceleration. Remove the forward force if the push has ended, or include a balancing backward force if a forward interaction continues; also include vertical weight/support as appropriate.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Evidence/job: 1.5-model-critique

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Question 19

Practice Set 3 · DOK 3 · mixed · U1-MG04

Do the scenario, motion description, and force model agree? Identify the mismatch and revise one representation.

Answer / solution

They do not agree. The diagram has a 40 N net force right, which would change the velocity. For constant straight-line speed, revise the forces so the horizontal net is 0 N, such as 80 N right and 80 N left.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

The force model should have zero net force, with support/tension balancing weight.

A hanging lamp is motionless. Choose the object as the system and list the external forces that belong on its force diagram.

Answer / solution

Forces on the lamp include weight downward and tension/support upward.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.

Evidence/job: 1.5-force-model-construct

Mastery Goal: U1-MG04 — Create, critique, and defend force models for real-world systems using evidence about interactions and motion.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.5 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

Warm-Up 1

Warm-Up 1 Question 1

Warm-Up 1 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG04

A cart’s velocity remains 3 m/s east for several seconds. Use the motion evidence to decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

Answer / solution

The velocity is constant, so the net force is zero.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.

Warm-Up 1 Question 2

Warm-Up 1 · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG04

A car accelerates forward on a level road. Describe a defensible force model and connect it to the motion evidence.

Answer / solution

A defensible model includes balanced vertical forces and a forward net horizontal force from interactions with the road/drag considered at course level.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Warm-Up 2 Question 4

Warm-Up 2 · DOK 2 · mixed · U1-MG04

The cart rolls at constant speed after a push. Critique the shown force model and describe a revision consistent with the motion.

Answer / solution

A constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. A lone forward force would predict acceleration. Remove the forward force if the push has ended, or include a balancing backward force if a forward interaction continues; also include vertical weight/support as appropriate.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Exact I-can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Warm-Up 3 · DOK 2 · mixed · U1-MG04

Secure Summative

Six secure versions. Science profile: 16 selected-response + 4 constructed-response per version.

V1

V1 Question 1

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG01

What is the best interpretation of the relationship $v=d/t$?

A. It connects speed to distance covered per unit time; the symbols represent physical quantities.
B. It is only a calculator shortcut with no physical meaning.
C. It proves every object moves at constant speed.
D. It says distance and time are forces.
Answer / solution

It connects speed to distance covered per unit time; the symbols represent physical quantities.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Exact I-can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Evidence/job: V1-E01

Mastery Goal: U1-MG01 — Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.1 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

V1 Question 2

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG03

Two perpendicular forces are 30 N east and 40 N north. What is the magnitude of the resultant?

A. 50 N
B. 10 N
C. 70 N
D. 1200 N
Answer / solution

50 N

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

Exact I-can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Evidence/job: V1-E02

Mastery Goal: U1-MG03 — Represent and determine net force using vectors, then use the result to classify balanced and unbalanced situations.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.3 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

V1 Question 3

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG01

Which claim is most directly testable with a controlled measurement?

A. Increasing the applied pull on the same cart changes its motion more over the same time.
B. Objects move because nature prefers motion.
C. This metal is strong because it has powerful matter.
D. The universe tends to seek balance because it wants stability.
Answer / solution

Increasing the applied pull on the same cart changes its motion more over the same time.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Exact I-can: I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.

Evidence/job: V1-E03

Mastery Goal: U1-MG01 — Use evidence and models to distinguish observations, inferences, and testable physics explanations, and communicate what a representation or relationship means.

Source basis: Original Unit 1 Assessment Plan; Framework section 1.1 enrichment/reference packet; Universal Question Structure Toolkit

V1 Question 5

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

A puck moves east at constant velocity while the net force is zero. What does Newton’s First Law predict?

A. The puck must gradually stop because motion requires force.
B. An inertia force pushes the puck east.
C. The puck must speed up because it is already moving.
D. The puck continues with the same velocity unless a net external force acts.
Answer / solution

The puck continues with the same velocity unless a net external force acts.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Exact I-can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Evidence/job: V1-E05

Mastery Goal: U1-MG02 — Explain Newton’s First Law and inertia to predict when an object’s motion remains unchanged or changes.

V1 Question 8

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG02

A book rests on a table. Which description is most accurate?

A. Only weight acts because support is not a force.
B. An inertia force upward cancels weight.
C. Weight and support force both act, and their vector sum can be zero.

Weight and support force both act, and their vector sum can be zero.

V1 Question 20

Secure Summative · DOK 3 · model/data · U1-MG04

A delivery cart is observed moving right at constant speed. A student draws only one horizontal arrow labeled “forward force.” Critique the model and revise it so the diagram and motion evidence agree.

Answer / solution

The lone forward arrow implies a nonzero net force and conflicts with constant velocity. Revise to zero horizontal net force: remove the forward interaction if none acts or include a balancing backward force; include vertical forces as appropriate.

Secure Summative · DOK 2 · text · U1-MG01

Which claim is most directly testable with a controlled measurement?

A. Increasing the applied pull on the same cart changes its motion more over the same time.
B. Objects move because nature prefers motion.
C. This metal is strong because it has powerful matter.
D. The universe tends to seek balance because it wants stability.
Answer / solution

Increasing the applied pull on the same cart changes its motion more over the same time.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

Exact I-can: I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.

The stopwatch reading is an observation/measurement; the lubrication statement is an inference.

A sign hangs motionless while tension balances weight.

V6 Question 18

Secure Summative · DOK 3 · model/data · U1-MG02

A moving object has several nonzero forces acting on it but continues in a straight line at constant speed. Explain how that is possible and distinguish “no forces” from “no net force.”

Answer / solution

The forces can cancel vectorially so net force is zero. Nonzero individual forces may be present; no net force means their vector sum is zero.

Alignment / evidence

Exact target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

Exact I-can: I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

Rightward total = 43 N; leftward = 31 N; net = 12 N right, represented by one rightward resultant vector.
